speechtext:
It is not usual, Mr. Speaker, to ask without notice on the orders of the day a question of the character indicated, involving as it does international relations. Provision has been made within the last twelve months for special representatives of the Department of Trade and Commerce to take up location in China, and they have undertaken their duties there. I think the practice, Mr. Speaker, is not one that should be established in this house of asking questions prefaced by a statement alleged to be a statement of fact, because so far as one reading it in a journal is concerned it may have the effect of doing the very opposite of what the hon. gentleman desires.
I think the house should take cognizance of the fact that a telegram was read a few moments ago in which a statement was made as a statement of fact. It was a very serious statement. It may or may not be accurate. The rules indicate that such telegrams should not be read in this house at this stage.
The statement just made by the hon. gentleman if correct would involve a rather serious question. I suggest that we should be a bit careful in dealing with our international relations especially in times when great consequences often follow from very small beginnings in matters of this kind. I shall, however, look into the matter and advise the hon. gentleman, and if he has any desire to inform himself and will apply at the office I assure him that at all times I shall be glad to try to satisfy his very commendable curiosity.

For the benefit of the Prime Minister I might say that the information I received was contained in an address delivered by Mr. Leon Ladner of Vancouver, who told an audience that the interests of Canada suffered because she had not a representative in China.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman if it is in this item that the government has succeeded where others have failed? I should like to have a concrete case in order that I may know when it has happened.

speechtext: The particular article under this heading that is of interest to us is the first part, fencing, coated or not. speechtext: How much per hundred pounds?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It was $2.75 a hundred. I had to fence a half section at that time, and at my local point it cost $2.75 a hundredweight. We must have barbed wire; if stock is to be kept to any considerable extent it is one of our most essential requirements. In these days when farming is being carried on, not at a very small profit but at an absolute loss, why the government should see fit to impose this extra burden upon the purchaser of barbed wire I cannot understand. Of course we know -that the indicated purpose behind these treaties is to divert trade to Great Britain-

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

speechtext: That is what I understood, and this brings up not a potential situation or a matter of imagination or prophecy, but an actual fact. During the last week, no doubt in common with other hon. members, I have been in receipt of a number of telegrams and communications from consumers of barbed wire in western Canada, complaining of a recent and substantial increase in the retail cost of that commodity, which increase has come about within the last ten days. When the matter was brought up in the house a short time ago, I think by the hon. member for Battle River, I believe it was intimated that some action had been taken to stop the dumping of barbed wire into this country at unfair prices, but that the actual fair market price had not been altered in any way. There is no doubt in my mind that any increase in the price of barbed wire at the present time is serious. I think that will be admitted on every side. It is a fact that farming is being carried on at a loss, and the slightest increase in our cost of production is a matter of very grave consideration. In addition, every tendency today whether on the part of governments, of individuals or of organizations, is towards mixed farming, if possible getting away from that great overproduction of wheat and turning to other lines of agriculture. As a matter of fact, to a very large extent the agreement itself, so far as it concerns farm products, is based upon that increase in mixed farming. As the hon. member for Lisgar has said, and as everyone acquainted with western Canada knows, mixed farming there is practically dependent upon the increased use of barbed wire fencing. It cannot be otherwise. Barbed wire forms a very substantial and an inescapable portion of the cost of farming, particularly if you go into cattle raising or other forms of mixed farming. I think the house is as one in deploring anything that may increase the cost of this commodity, but whether it is a result of the treaty or a most unfortunate coincidence, the fact remains that the price has gone up, and that from every side we are receiving complaints. This increase may be due to the fact that dumping has been stopped; v'e do not know. The farmer does know, however, that the price has increased and that he is paying more for his barbed ware.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend any
information as to the extent of the increase complained of?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I think I can get that information, though most of the wires simply complain without giving very definite statistics. I did not bring those telegrams with me because I did not know this item was coming up today, but I think one or two of them contain actual figures. Certainly definite statements have been made, and in some cases they are backed up by exact figures as to prices paid.
It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that it is an almost inescapable inference at least, with these tariffs having been in effect for the past three or four weeks, that the increase in price is a direct result. Rightly or wrongly that is the inference drawn, whether it is a necessary increase or whether the retailers are taking advantage of the situation. I do not know what are the facts, and the farmers do not know, but they do know that the price has gone up. If that is the inevitable result of this agreement then I think this is one point that certainly must be discussed and if possible corrected, because the whole argument in favour of the British preference is that it will result in the diversion of trade -which I for one should be very glad to see- but that this diversion of trade will be made without increasing the cost to the consumer
1266	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
or placing an additional burden upon those who may use the articles imported. There is the whole difficulty. If the treaty has this result it will not be the foreigner who will pay the cost of the agreement; it will be paid by the consumer here. If that is to be the result the whole basis is wrong.
I will not go further, but I am asking the minister to institute as soon as possible the most careful inquiry into the matter. I am not asking him to take my statement; I am not even asking him to accept any telegrams that may be sent, because at times they are wholly unreliable. In view of the statement that prices have increased, and the widespread complaints that have been made, together with the fact that it is of such great importance to have these prices as low as possible without inflicting injury upon anyone, I ask the minister to look into the matter. We want barbed wire to be sold at the lowest possible legitimate price, and in view of these facts I ask the government to make the fullest inquiry. If they find that someone has been attempting to exploit the consumer as a result of this tariff, or that under this tariff we cannot get barbed wire as cheaply as we formerly could, I ask the government to use the powers contained in the treaty and remedy that injustice, if any has been brought about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am going to intervene
in this debate, Mr. Chairman, merely to make a very few observations. The hon. member for Red Deer used the words "as low as it can be purchased legitimately." I suppose he is aware of the fact that during the past several months in this country barbed wire has been dumped on the Canadian market from the Netherlands. As a matter of fact, the wire was brought from Germany unbarbed into the Netherlands and then barbed and shipped here by water to Vancouver. The price at which it has been sold was admittedly a dump price. It is only necessary to point out to the committee that the entire requirements of Canadians for barbed wire have been met practically by Canadians.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Quite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Red Deer is fair enough to admit that that is correct, and I commend that to the hon. member for Lisgar. Now, the total importation, when barbed wire was free across the board, was not $85,000.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It was
as high as $125,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I was coming to that. It did reach a maximum of $125,000 but the average was something like $85,000. But Canadians have supplied their own requirements in barbed wire and have had keen competition with the whole world. Recently however barbed wire has been dumped upon the Canadian market by foreigners to destroy Canadian industry, just cold-bloodedly-admittedly in cold blood. I will give the committee an illustration. Not long since orders were taken for Canadian barbed wire. The Dutch interests have in this country a representative in the person of Mr. Leith Murray. They went so far as to say, "We will undersell you, whatever your price may be. Substantially that will be the effect. There will be no dumping duty on it and we will sell this Dutch wire in this country regardless." Now, the price at which the Canadian is selling barbed wire at the present moment is $2.32 per hundred pounds, while the price in the United States is $2.60. The competition formerly was between the United States and Canada, and the Canadian interests were able to purchase barbed wire delivered at the head of the lakes, in competition with Pittsburgh wire delivered at the head of the lakes, when the item was on the free list, and undersell them. I well recall-I was not actively interested in politics at the time and was not in the house-that Mr. Walton, manager of the largest wholesale firm in Canada, Marshall, Wells & Company, explained to me the extent to which we Canadians were producing our own requirements, and he pointed out barbed wire as an illustration. Being free across the board, it was being produced by Canadians cheaper than it could be delivered by the American producers in the United States.
There has arisen however a situation which is entirely different from that. A foreign interest has resolved to destroy the Canadian market-

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Maliciously?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I did not say that. The hon. gentleman can hardly conceive anything not being done that way. I did say however that they have resolved to do it, and having resolved to do it they set out by reducing prices to accomplish that end.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Could not that be met by means of ordinary dumping duties?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
One of the difficulties is to determine how you can apply the dumping duty to certain commodities. In the Netherlands there is no market for barbed wire, and

United Kingdom
to find a fair market price for barbed wire where there is no sale for the commodity is an exceedingly difficult thing, and section 36 of the Customs Act, to which the hon. gentleman refers, contemplates the sale being made cheaper than the sale that is made to the people of the country in which the commodity is produced. Owing to the fact that the wire itself comes from Germany and is barbed in the Netherlands, and that there is no market at all in the Netherlands for barbed wire, you cannot apply that section, which contemplates the ascertaining of the domestic price for the commodity and then comparing that with the price for which the commodity is being offered in the country to which it is exported.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Why was this tariff change not postponed until the regular budget came down, instead of putting it here under the guise of a British preference, which, as I see it, is absolutely useless.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Presently I shall deal with that phase of the situation. Perhaps I might do so now. Great Britain sold only $10,000 in our market in a given period. Larger quantities were sold by Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium. Those are the four countries from which our importations came, the United States being $34,000, larger, as a matter of fact, than any of the other three. Now, the position is this. If Great Britain could supply it we should prefer to buy it from Great Britain. We have never made any bones about that, to use a colloquial expression. There has been no raising of the price by the Canadian producer, none at all. His price is $2.32 and the American price at the moment is $2.60. It is difficult to ascertain the market price for barbed wire in a country where barbed wire has no sale. It has in Germany, and the domestic price there bears a close relation to our own. As most hon. members know, barbed wire is not used in Great Britain commercially as it is here, and in the Netherlands there is no market at all.
When this matter was presented for our consideration we said, "We will make it free, but we must at least see that the British producer has an even chance as compared with those who are dumping their product on this market." I had occasion to point this out the other day. A few years ago the entire agricultural production in Canada, including fruit and vegetables and every form of agricultural activity, embracing live stock as well, amounted, roughly, to $1,600,000,000, of which only $300,000,000 worth was exported. The other $1,300,000,000 were consumed by 10,000,000 people, indicating of course that the
domestic market is still by all odds the great market for Canadian producers-the very greatest market there is.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Have you made allowance for duplications?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I merely take the figures as the statistical department have prepared them, and I have every reason to believe that under Doctor Coats' direction every possible likelihood of erroneous figures being produced has been eliminated. I can only give them as they are. I have the figures for the last three years, but I take the round figures for one year, and as I have said, of $1,600,000,000, roughly, we exported $299,000,000, or, to use round figures, $300,000,000, leaving $1,300,000,000 of agricultural products consumed by 10,000,000 people

that is, before England went off the gold standard. The very essence of the maintenance of some form of industrial life in this country is to maintain that domestic market, and to do that we must give a fair chance to industry, just as the agriculturist has asked for an even chance with New Zealand butter or Australian products, or in relation to any form of agricultural activity whatever it may be. The Canadian producer says, "All I want is a fair chance in my own market." Now, when you find Canadian barbed wire being sold to Canadians at 28 cents per hundred pounds less than in the United States, and when you find, so far as you can ascertain, that the price at which barbed wire is being offered in the Netherlands is lower than the cost of production, on any fair basis of production costs, are you not bound to take steps to give the Canadian a fair chance, and to give the Englishman that chance as well? We have said to the Englishman, "We will make it free and give you a fair chance, that is, even competition with the Canadian," and if he has an even chance in this market with the Canadian, why should we be so solicitous about those who are making no contribution to our welfare?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
What about the farmers?
It is the farmers of whom we are solicitous.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The farmers, if the situation is left to work out its logical conclusion, will eventually pay any price the foreigner may demand.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
They can't live that
long.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Someone says they cannot live that long, but I have seen Canadian industry destroyed and the foreigner fix prices. My hon. friend from Red Deer used the word
126S	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
legitimately and used it properly, and I can see that he meant that if there were not an even chance afforded either to his own country or to Great Britain with respect to this commodity it was not legitimate nor fair. It is to overcome the dumping practice in this market in connection with barbed wire that this step is being taken, and the only method by which that could be accomplished is this. You may think you have devised other methods, but this is the only really effective method that will do it; and if, as the hon. member for Red Deer has found, a hardship is worked in any particular class, the agreement is provided to meet that situation, just as it has done with respect to one or two other matters, since the agreements were signed, both in Australia and elsewhere. I think I could give more striking illustrations of what has happened recently in connection with orders that were given to Canadian producers of barbed wire, the base price being $2.32. Those who have given the orders have been asked by the Dutch agents in this country to cancel them and to substitute Dutch wire, made first in Germany, barbed in the Netherlands, and shipped to Canada by water, to supplant the Canadian product made by Canadian people who consume a part of that $1,300,000,000 which constitutes the largest market the Canadian farmer has for his product-the home market.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The very fact that the great percentage of our market is supplied by Canadian industry would indicate that any increased cost of importation, supposing it were brought about, should have no effect upon the price. That is, if the price were being raised in Canada, I mean apart from any temporary and unfair dumping of which I am not speaking at the moment, this would show that the industry or part of the industry or the retailers under the industry were taking unnecessary advantage of the tariff, because it is not the imported article that sets the price. I am merely asking that under the circumstances the government ascertain whether in any districts there has been an unnecessary increase in the legitimate price and that, if so, they take the necessary steps.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I assure the hon. gentleman that this is a matter in which I had considerable interest. My information at the moment is that there has been no increase in price by Canadians, but the foreigner, taking advantage of the situation, has been endeavouring to get a higher price on the theory that he now has a monopoly of the market, having cancelled the orders of the Canadian

producers and driven them out. If that is what the committee wants to have done, all they have to do is to make it clear. They will not get it so far as this government is concerned.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The Prime Minister directed a remark to me commending the attitude of the hon. member for Red Deer when he admitted the larger proportion of our requirements was provided from the Canadian market. I did not need to admit that definitely when I pointed out that we had a very small proportion-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
From Great Britain.
Mr. BROWN -from Great Britain, another small proportion of our requirements from foreign countries and some $550,000 worth from Canada, which in itself is an indication that we are getting most of our requirements from our own producers. Therefore I do not think the Prime Minister need emphasize the point that my attitude should be the same as that of the hon. member for Red Deer. The Prime Minister has made another very interesting admission, namely that Canadian manufacturers of barbed wire have been providing for Canadian requirements in competition with the United States, and they have been doing that for thirty-five years without a duty.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: No.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I know whereof I speak. Barbed wire was put on the free list by the first Fielding tariff in 1897. I had occasion, as I well remember when I was fencing my farm about which I spoke, to come into contact with a very strong protectionist who was complaining that the Fielding tariff had not reduced duties at all. I immediately pointed to what I had done in fencing my own farm at the price I have already indicated, because of the reduction that was brought about in the price of barbed wire by the Fielding tariff. He said: "Oh, that was the worst thing that was done for Canada." I said: "You cannot have it both ways." He was arguing about the Fielding tariff having reduced no duties, and he was also complaining that it bad. This is characteristic of the arguments we are hearing these days from the other side of the house. I have been contending all these years that Canadian manufacturers could compete with other manufacturers without these large protective duties, and the Prime Minister has at least admitted the fact that for thirty-five years the Canadian manufacturer of barbed wire has been supplying the major portion of our requirements and yet barbed wire has been on the free list. When we are

United Kingdom
discussing this matter of prices, it should be borne in mind that I am speaking of retail prices I had to pay in my town, and probably the prices quoted by the Prime Minister are wholesale prices. We must not get confused over these matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
But the retail price is
not a matter over which the federal government has any control.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I admit that. When the
hon. member for Wentworth challenged the price I gave, he should remember he was giving the price in Ontario, very near to where the wire was made, and I was quoting the price away out on the prairie where it had to carry a large freight rate.

speechtext:
That shows that factories
are needed out there.

speechtext:
That is about as wise as
any other remarks made by the hon. gentleman. I was quoting a price that carried a very high freight rate, so that the statement of the hon. member for Wentworth is not necessarily a contradiction of mine.
Granting that the statements of the Prime Minister in regard to the situation that prevails in Holland are correct, why should this material be brought in under the guise of diverting trade to Great Britain? Why should it have been made a part of this imperial agreement? If the situation which he describes needed to be met, it was quite possible to meet it in some other way and not to include this item in an agreement to which we are bound for a period of five years. That is one point to which we object.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
May I answer a point
raised by the hon. member for Red Deer? Since he spoke I have received definite information that neither by the manufacturer nor by one of the large distributors throughout western Canada has there been any increase in the cost of barbed wire in the period mentioned.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Is any safeguard being
provided against increases?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It is possible that the
communications which I and others have received refer only to the stopping of temporary dumping. I am not making any assertion as to that. I am simply stating the facts as to the prices paid. May I, while I am on my feet, express my agreement with one point raised by the hon. member for Lisgar? If these tariffs had for their purpose not so much the diversion of trade as the protection of Canadian industry from unfair dumping, I
certainly think it would have been far better, with that end in view, to introduce the item definitely as part of the Canadian tariff which may be altered at our discretion at any time, instead of making it part of the agreement.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am sorry the Prime Minister has left his seat. While he was speaking I took down some of the figures he quoted. He spoke of $1,300,000,000 worth of Canadian farm products being consumed by 10,000,000 people in a year. I asked him if he had made any allowance for duplications, and he said the figures he gave were accurate. This would mean $130 worth consumed annually by every man, woman and child in Canada, or $650 worth for a family, in addition to tea, coffee, tropical fruits and such other foodstuffs as we bring in from abroad. It does not require any close scrutiny of the figures to realize there is something wrong with them. If the Prime Minister's information as to what is going on in Holland in connection with barbed wire is no more accurate than his information in connection with the consumption by the Canadian people of foodstuffs grown on Canadian farms, then I think he is acting without sufficient information in raising these tariffs. The imports of barbed wire were $125,000 from all sources, of which $10,000 came from the United Kingdom, leaving $115,000 coming in from abroad. The Canadian production, the minister tells us, was $535,000. The total consumption in Canada must therefore be $660,000 worth, of which $115,000 comes in from abroad. In order to divert that $115,000 worth which comes in from abroad, and only $33,000 of it comes in from Holland, either to the United Kingdom or Canadian factories, we, the people of Canada, are going to pay an extra 10 per cent on the whole $660,000 worth, or $66,000.

43. My hon. friend has never got disentangled mentally or any other way, that is the trouble. The Prime Minister made a very complete statement of the situation and I am not going to repeat it. In regard to this question of barbed wire there is no doubt that during the past year or more Canada has been subjected to unfair practices in trade. That applies not only to barbed wire but to other commodities. It is an unfortunate condition that exists in the world, it is not peculiar to Canada. It arises out of a quite well-known economic condition; merchants all over the world find themselves in possession of large stocks of goods, or in possession of plants that they desire to keep going. I presume Canadian producers would do the same thing. If they can dump their excess products on some other market and thus maintain at least a salvage price for that portion, so as to cut down the percentage of overhead on the whole, they do so. It has been a practice, a bad practice, a very embarrassing practice, and one which the whole world is now studying with a view to getting rid of. We were faced with this condition. My hon. friend from Red Deer was fair enough in his observations to say that he did not advocate that Canadian consumers should take advantage of a condition of that kind, he was satisfied if the ordinary principles of fair trade were observed. Now the Prime Minister indicated this problem, and my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth laughed at him. The Prime Minister properly said that it was very difficult to secure under section 6 of the Customs Act, the dumping clause, the evidence upon which that clause might be applied. That is for the very simple reason that barbed wire has no local sale in Belgium that would enable this government to fix the sale price in that country. "But," the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth says, "that does not matter; why did you not invoke section 43?" That is a different section altogether, and in this case we did not desire or choose to invoke section 43. Here we have this arrangement by which we give an advantage to the British manufacturer in this market. The Canadian consumer is ensured fair treatment for two reasons: First, he has had fair treatment in the past from the Canadian manufacturer and there is no indication that this will be changed; in the second place he has the competition of the British producer as a check upon the Canadian manufacturer. I think I can say with some degree of assurance, based upon the experience we have had in the past, that the consumer of barbed wire need have

no apprehension with regard to increased prices due to this tariff. I agree with my colleague the Minister of Finance when he says that whether they be products of the farm, of the mine or of the forest, or the general products of industry in this country, I sincerely hope all commodities experience a substantial increase in value within the next year or two. I think there is not a country in the world, or any government, or any leader of agriculture or industry, but will join in the fervent expectation and desire that commodity prices will increase, so I would not for a moment say thait the prices of barbed wire will not increase in the next two or three years. I hope barbed wire will increase in price, as my colleague has said, just as I hope wheat, butter, lumber, copper, iron, fish and all other products will increase in price.

Mr. Chairman, could there be an example more palpable than this of endeavouring to increase the tariff under the pretext of giving Great Britain an increased preference? The British preferential rate remains at 20 per cent, the same as it was previously. If the government had wished to give a real preference to Great Britain they could have lowered the tariff to 15 per cent or 10 per cent. But instead of doing that they shove up a tariff standing at the high figure of 30 per cent, making it 35 per cent. Further, they changed the intermediate rate
LMr. Mackenzie King]
from 27i per cent to 30 per cent. This is an instance of simply increasing protection without in any way helping the Britisher.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: This, as the exMinister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has said, is just another instance of tariffs being made to fight against the farmer. The item relates to articles which enter into agricultural implements. The policy of the late Liberal administration was to free agricultural implements from duty as far as possible, and this item was free all across. Hon. gentlemen have left it where it was under the British preference, but they have put the duty up to 10 per cent in the intermediate and 10 per cent in the general. The minister has just shown what a small proportion came from Great Britain compared with the amount imported from other countries. It is another instance of a tariff for manufacturers, made by manufacturers, and put on the statutes by a manufacturers' government.

Another allegation was that this will merely result in an increase in the price. I am going to deal briefly with both those points, but I hope as completely as necessary. First may I say that Canada will have access to other markets for cream separators. That should be borne in mind. Cream separators were introduced into this country, as far as Great Britain is concerned, about forty years ago, and it is rather interesting to know that the head of the firm which introduced the first cream separator into Canada at that time, was R. A. Lister of the R. A. Lister Company. I had a call the other day from the son of the gentleman who was and I assume still is the head of this firm, and had an opportunity of discussing the question with him from the standpoint of trade with Great Britain. This company sold very substantial quantities of
cream separators to Canada. The history of the business is divided into pre-war and post war periods. This old country firm manufactured cream separators very extensively up to the outbreak of the war, when they turned their plant over to the British government for the manufacture of munitions, and the exportation of cream separators to Canada virtually stopped. They have exported some few to this country since. I submit to the committee in the first place that the British manufacturers of cream separators are competent to effectively supply this market. speechtext:
I suppose
the machines exported are United States machines.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Not all, but I presume
they were mainly United States machines; I think it would be safe to say that the great proportion of our re-export would be machines of American manufacture.
The point I am making is that in this business there is a capacity for expansion, both Canadian and British, without doing any injury to either the consumer or the producer in this country. As I have already indicated, we have received an added advantage in the markets of the other parts of the empire, and we are giving to Great Britain an advantage in this market so far as foreign competition is concerned. At the same time we have already developed in Canada a very healthy and substantial business in the production of cream separators. I questioned the gentleman with whom I spoke as to the price at which Great Britain could lay down those cream separators here; I must say that he spoke with reasonable reserve and I felt safe in putting confidence in what he said. He assured me that not only could they supply the market, but that the price would not be advanced over the price that had been paid for foreign separators as well as for their own. He told me there was no possibility or danger or likelihood of an increase in price because of this adjustment. I think they fully appreciate the value of this market for cream separators, and today are arranging for sales organizations throughout the country for the purpose of selling these machines.

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Did he disclose to the minister the reason why the British manufacturer got out of the market?

subtopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Yes, he did, and I am
glad my hon. friend mentioned that. He said they lost their business during the war because they turned their factory over for the production of war materials. During that period they were agents for a Swedish cream separator company, and in their foreign business they acted for that company. While I am not certain who was the chief exporter to Canada of the cream separators recorded as from Sweden, I am reasonably sure that it was from this particular firm. Having got back into business again, they are now prepared from their British factory to supply this market in quantity.
